summary: This document defines a YANG data model for the delivery of Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPN services. It covers BGP PE-based VPNs and is meant for communication between customers and network operators, instantiated at the operator's management system.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8299 defines a YANG model that lets a customer describe a Layer 3 virtual private network (VPN) service to a provider. The provider's management system uses that request to configure network devices; the model itself is not installed on those devices.

subtitle: A YANG model for describing a Layer 3 VPN service to a network operator.

tldr.problem: Customers and network operators need a shared way to describe a Layer 3 VPN service without specifying each router's configuration.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8299 defines the ietf-l3vpn-svc YANG model for VPN services, customer sites, and their network accesses. A management system turns those service details into device-specific configuration.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8299 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8049. It replaces that unimplementable module with a new module of the same name that is not backward compatible.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 8299 defines a Layer 3 VPN service data model written in YANG. Customers and network operators can use it to describe service settings, and automated management applications can use those settings as input.

The model covers BGP Provider Edge (PE)-based VPNs. It describes an abstract service, not the configuration of individual network devices. A management system must translate the service description into device-specific configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines a shared way to describe a provider-managed Layer 3 VPN service. It covers BGP PE-based VPNs and leaves the actual router configuration to the provider's management system.

sections.title: The Model Runs in a Management System
sections.content:
The service model is intended to sit between a customer's system and a network operator's management system. In the described arrangement, the customer's system is the client and the operator's system is the server. The model can also feed an orchestration layer that coordinates service configuration.

The management system translates the request into configuration for network elements, such as routers or servers. It may use NETCONF, RESTCONF, a command-line interface, or another method chosen by the operator. The RFC does not specify how those elements are configured.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer sends a service description to the provider's management system. That system decides how to configure the network equipment, using methods the RFC does not define.

sections.title: VPN Services, Sites and Network Accesses
sections.content:
The ietf-l3vpn-svc module has two main containers: vpn-services and sites. A VPN service entry holds general settings for a customer's VPN. A site describes a customer location that connects to one or more VPN services.

Each site has at least one site-network-access; a site can have more than one, including for multihoming. Each access has a bearer for attachment properties below Layer 3 and an ip-connection for Layer 3 settings. The access also carries service and availability details. If a setting is supplied both for a site and for one of its accesses, the access-level setting MUST take precedence.
sections.plainLanguage: The model records VPN-wide settings, customer sites, and each site's connections to the provider. A site can have several connections, and a setting on one connection overrides the same setting inherited from the site.

sections.title: VPN Topologies and Site Attachments
sections.content:
The model supports three VPN topologies: any-to-any, Hub and Spoke, and Hub and Spoke disjoint. Any-to-any is the default and lets all sites communicate without restrictions. In Hub and Spoke, Spokes communicate only with Hubs while Hubs can also communicate with one another; in the disjoint version, Hubs cannot communicate with one another.

Each site access must attach to a VPN, either by naming that VPN directly or by referencing a VPN policy. A policy can attach one or more VPNs and can use filters to send selected LANs to particular VPNs. The site role must match the chosen VPN topology.
sections.plainLanguage: A VPN can let every site communicate, or limit communication to Hub and Spoke roles. Each connection names its VPN directly or uses a policy for more complex membership.

sections.title: Choosing Where Each Access Connects
sections.content:
The management system chooses where each site access joins the provider network, such as a PE. It MUST honor customer constraints. If it cannot satisfy them, it MUST NOT provision the site and MUST report which constraints could not be met. Location and requested access type can guide placement, while the provider may also use internal criteria such as load or distance.

Customers can group accesses and request that they use different PEs, points of presence (POPs), line cards, or bearer components. They can also require accesses to share a PE or bearer. For multihomed sites, an access priority expresses preference: equal values can represent load sharing, while different values can represent primary and backup connections.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider must meet the customer's connection constraints or report that it cannot place an access. Priorities can indicate which connections should share traffic or act as backups.

sections.title: Connection and Service Choices
sections.content:
The model describes IPv4 and IPv6 connection settings, including five address-allocation methods: provider DHCP, provider DHCP relay, static addresses, Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), and provider DHCP with SLAAC. SLAAC options apply only to IPv6. It also supports routing choices including BGP, RIP, OSPF, static routing, direct connection, and VRRP.

For each access, the customer can describe bandwidth in the input and output directions, a maximum transmission unit (MTU), and quality-of-service (QoS) settings. QoS rules classify traffic in a user-defined order and assign it to a service class. The operator can apply a standard QoS profile or a custom profile with class properties such as direction, rate limit, latency, jitter, and bandwidth.

The model also defines provider-managed, customer-managed, and co-managed arrangements for customer edge (CE) equipment. These choices determine where the management boundary sits and which connection the routing settings describe.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer can specify how addresses are assigned, which routing protocol to use, and the access bandwidth. Ordered QoS rules sort traffic into service classes, and the model records who manages the customer equipment.

sections.title: Optional VPN Services
sections.content:
Optional service settings include access to public cloud services, multicast, and extranet VPNs. Cloud access can use NAT44, the only address-translation option defined here, and can allow or deny access for selected sites. By default, all sites in the VPN are authorized to access the cloud.

For multicast, the model records customer tree types and related parameters; if the service requests Any-Source Multicast, Rendezvous Point settings are required. An extranet setting lets one VPN request access to another VPN's resources. The RFC warns that when one VPN lists another as an extranet, all sites in the second VPN gain access to all sites in the first.

These settings describe service intent. How the provider implements cloud restrictions, multicast, or extranet connectivity on network elements is outside the RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The model can describe cloud access, multicast, and links between VPNs. It records the requested service, but leaves the network configuration for these features to the provider.

sections.title: Why RFC 8299 Replaces RFC 8049
sections.content:
RFC 8299 obsoletes RFC 8049 and gives the replacement YANG module the same name. The earlier module could be compiled as YANG but could not be implemented because some XPath expressions were broken. Other tools that parsed those expressions refused to compile the module.

The revision also resolves contradictions in how access-control-list rules were described and ordered, and makes other small fixes and clarifications. The new module is not backward compatible with RFC 8049. The RFC says the name was retained because the earlier module could not be implemented, so clients and servers could not have interoperated using it.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 8049 described a module that could not be implemented because of errors in its expressions. RFC 8299 fixes those problems, keeps the module name, and does not promise compatibility with the earlier module.

sections.title: Protecting Service Data and Requests
sections.content:
The RFC expects the model's data to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF. It identifies SSH as the mandatory secure transport for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF. The NETCONF access-control model can restrict which operations and data particular users may access.

Changes to VPN-service and site data can indirectly change PE and CE configurations, which could disrupt service or cause network misbehavior. These data also contain confidential customer information, such as names, locations, and subscribed services, so both read and write access need protection. For customer-provided encryption profiles, the model supports a pre-shared key and the RFC says to use a secure channel to prevent interception.
sections.plainLanguage: Service records can reveal customer details and can affect network configuration. The RFC calls for secure management connections and access controls to protect that information and prevent unwanted changes.
